steps.title: Setting goals
teach: Goal setting suits clients who are ready to change (Level 3, and sometimes Level 2). It breaks a big change into small steps, and each small success builds confidence. Goal setting is part of the Nutrition Care Process, Social Cognitive Theory and motivational interviewing.

Start with a broad goal, such as eating more fruit, then narrow it down to one specific, measurable, time-bound step. Many clients pick goals that are too ambitious. Help them find the smallest goal that is achievable and worthwhile, rather than asking how much they think they can do.

act.prompt: A client wants to “eat healthier from now on.” What's the best next step?

options.label: Ask how much she thinks she can change this week
options.feedback: This often leads to over-ambitious goals.

options.label: Help her find the smallest goal that is achievable and worthwhile
Keep the goal broad so it's flexible
options.feedback: Broad goals need to be narrowed to a specific step.

steps.title: Dietary assessment tools
teach: A 24-hour recall is quick, but people over- or under-report. Ask neutral questions like “What were the first foods or drinks you had after waking up?” rather than “What did you have for breakfast?”, which assumes a meal. A food frequency questionnaire shows how often foods are eaten. In a clinical setting, pairing it with a 24-hour recall gives a better picture.

A food diary (record) is filled in by the client and can also work as an intervention, because writing things down makes people more aware of their habits. Detailed history forms give clues to strengths and barriers, but some clients may find them invasive or culturally uncomfortable.

options.label: “What did you eat for breakfast?”
options.feedback: This assumes the client ate breakfast.

options.label: “What were the first foods or drinks you had after waking up today?”
options.feedback: Yes. It doesn't assume a meal was eaten.

steps.title: Estimating portions
teach: Everyday objects help clients estimate portions. Half a cup of fruit, vegetables, cooked cereal, pasta or rice is about a small fist. Three ounces of cooked meat, poultry or fish is about a deck of cards. A potato is about the size of a computer mouse.
Using these comparisons in recalls and food records makes estimates more accurate.

act.prompt: Match each portion with its everyday comparison.

items.label: ½ cup cooked rice
items.feedback: Half a cup is about a small fist.

items.label: 3 oz cooked chicken
items.feedback: Three ounces of meat is about a deck of cards.

items.label: A small baked potato
items.feedback: A potato is about the size of a computer mouse.

steps.title: Body weight standards
teach: Height–weight tables are outdated and no longer seen as a reliable way to find a healthy weight. BMI is used instead, but cut-offs vary by population. The World Health Organization suggests 23 as the overweight cut-off and 27.5 for obesity for most Asians. For Pacific Islanders, the overweight cut-off is 26.
BMI isn't a good guide to body fat in pregnant or breastfeeding women, very muscular people, growing children or adults over 65.

act.prompt: What BMI does the WHO suggest as the overweight level for Pacific Islanders?

options.feedback: 23 is the suggested cut-off for most Asians.
27.5 is the obesity cut-off for most Asians.
